title: Ten fast ways to edit Ports inside a Block
brief: Make adding, reordering, and deleting semantic ports extremely fast from within the Block window itself, while preserving the existing port-as-cable-terminal interaction. The comparison deliberately includes Zach's table-inspired hover/hold/context-menu hybrid and the proposed elbow-control-point model.
defaultWhy: Port Tool is the provisional default at 93.4/100. It is the only direction that combines top-tier repeated-edit throughput, dense-list/accessibility strength, and a completely explicit gesture boundary: one P/Ports entry amortizes across the edit burst, while ordinary port dragging remains exclusively cable creation outside the mode.
decisionHinge: The recommendation depends on burst throughput versus zero-learning visibility. Move 13 weight points from Repeated-edit throughput to First-use discoverability and V10 Footer Strip narrowly leads V3 (91.0 vs 90.8). If a typical session makes one port edit, choose V10; if it makes several, keep V3. V1 Boundary Rows is the best gesture layer to splice on top of either command baseline.
invariants: Use the same selected decode Block in Port view with in_1 and out_1, then demonstrate adding in_2, moving it above in_1, and deleting out_1.
Inputs remain on the left edge and outputs on the right; port order is semantic and survives Port ↔ Expanded view changes.
A normal drag from a port terminal continues to start a semantic cable unless an unmistakable port-edit state owns the gesture.
Deleting a connected port must make the affected cable count explicit and remain one-step undoable.
All port mutations address stable ids and commit through the same command layer used by the inspector and context menu.
boundary: Standalone interactive front-end slices at a shared SystemSketch-like Block fidelity. Guided stories, direct add/move/delete controls, prune state, and export work in the gallery; real tldraw pointer capture, cable bindings, touch thresholds, command dispatch, undo, persistence, and Port/Expanded integration are simulated and require production validation after selection.

requirements.name: Repeated-edit throughput
requirements.why: Zach's stated outcome is a very fast on-canvas loop for creating, arranging, and removing several ports—not merely one successful edit.
requirements.passCondition: After the mechanism is known, add, reorder, and delete each take one short action and several edits can be chained without leaving the Block.

anchors.1: Each edit requires leaving the canvas or reopening a deep surface.
anchors.3: Each operation is available, but repeated edits accumulate menu, targeting, or mode overhead.
anchors.5: All three operations chain as direct one-action edits at the Block.

requirements.name: Zero gesture ambiguity
requirements.why: A port already owns the cable-drag gesture, while the Block owns selection and text editing. Inline editing must not make those common actions feel unreliable.
requirements.passCondition: The user can predict whether a pointer action selects, wires, edits text, reorders, or deletes before committing it.

anchors.1: Common wiring or selection gestures can accidentally mutate the port list.
anchors.3: Conflicts are reduced with timing, modifiers, or target precision but remain learnable hazards.
anchors.5: Port-list mutation has an unmistakable target or bounded mode and ordinary canvas gestures stay intact.

requirements.name: First-use discoverability
requirements.why: The Block should teach the interaction through familiar visible affordances rather than rely on remembered shortcuts or documentation.
requirements.passCondition: A new user hovering or selecting the Block can identify how to add a port and infer where reorder/delete live.

anchors.1: The interaction is invisible unless the user already knows a shortcut or gesture.
anchors.3: One entry point is visible, but the full operation set is hidden behind convention or exploration.
anchors.5: Visible labels, handles, or familiar row controls make all three operations self-explanatory.

requirements.name: Canvas continuity
requirements.why: The point of this feature is to stay in the window and preserve spatial focus on the Block rather than detour into the inspector.
requirements.passCondition: The Block, target side, and neighboring ports remain visible while editing, with little temporary occlusion or chrome.

anchors.1: Editing replaces the canvas context or moves the task to a distant surface.
anchors.3: The interaction stays anchored but meaningfully covers the Block or surrounding sketch.
anchors.5: Edits happen directly at the port boundary with the full local sketch context intact.

requirements.name: Precision, access, and scale
requirements.why: Expanded Blocks may hold dense port lists, and the same capability should remain usable with keyboard, touch/pen, zoom, and reduced dexterity.
requirements.passCondition: Targets remain precise at dense scales and every operation has an explicit keyboard- or command-invocable path.

anchors.1: Tiny targets, timing, or unsupported input devices make the operation unreliable.
anchors.3: The common mouse case works, but density or alternate input needs a fallback surface.
anchors.5: Large targets, keyboard parity, and list behavior remain robust across dense Port and Expanded views.

hardGates.name: Cable drag remains unambiguous
hardGates.why: Dragging a port is already how semantic cables start; a winning edit model cannot silently steal that gesture.

hardGates.name: Connected delete is explicit and undoable
hardGates.why: Removing a connected port changes topology; the affected cable count must be visible and the mutation must be recoverable in one undo.

hardGates.name: Port and Expanded parity
hardGates.why: The same mental model must work on the compact Port face and the spatially stretched Expanded frame.

hardGates.name: Stable identity and one history step
hardGates.why: Reorder must preserve durable port IDs and each add/move/delete commit must map cleanly onto tldraw undo/redo.

variants.name: Boundary Rows
variants.thesis: Use Zach's table-inspired hybrid: hover gaps to insert, press-hold a row grip to reorder, and right-click for explicit row commands.
variants.bestWhen: The priority is maximum pointer speed with familiar table grammar and the existing right-click command layer as a safety net.
variants.losesWhen: Hold timing and small boundary targets make pen, touch, or dense Expanded layouts feel unreliable.

decisions.label: Primary object
decisions.value: A port behaves like a table row whose boundary exposes insertion and whose gutter exposes ordering.

decisions.label: Reorder
decisions.value: Press-hold on the row gutter crosses a drag threshold; a normal click still selects.

decisions.label: Delete
decisions.value: The row menu names affected cables and exposes Delete plus Undo.

proof: The live hero adds in_2 at a gap, moves it above in_1, and removes out_1 through its row affordance.
The reference strip shows the exact Block, Obsidian table insertion, and row-menu sources Zach supplied.

fr1.evidence: Gap add, held row grip, and row menu all remain at the Block and can chain without opening the inspector.

fr2.evidence: A distinct gutter helps, but reorder still depends on a hold threshold that can be confused with selection or a slow cable drag.

fr3.evidence: The visible plus, six-dot grip, and familiar row menu expose the complete operation set.

fr4.evidence: Every action stays on the boundary and the Block remains visible.

fr5.evidence: The menu provides keyboard fallback, but hover gaps and hold timing remain precision-sensitive.

g1.evidence: The reorder grip is outside the port dot, so the cable terminal keeps its direct drag gesture.

g2.evidence: The row menu can show ‘Delete out_1 · 1 cable’ and produce a single Undo toast.

g3.evidence: The row/gap grammar projects onto both compact and stretched edges.

g4.evidence: Moving rows changes list order while the stable port id remains unchanged.

variants.name: Perimeter Beads
variants.thesis: Treat ports like elbow control points: selected Blocks reveal occupied beads and hollow gap beads directly on the perimeter.
variants.bestWhen: The geometric edge itself should be the entire mental model and pointer users value minimal chrome.
variants.losesWhen: The same bead must mean both wire terminal and reorder handle, or the edge becomes too dense to target reliably.

decisions.label: Primary object
decisions.value: The Block perimeter is a control-point rail, not a list of rows.

decisions.label: Add and move
decisions.value: Click a hollow bead to add; drag an occupied bead to a new slot.

decisions.label: Delete
decisions.value: Alt-click or drag a bead to a perimeter trash notch.

proof: The live hero exposes a hollow insertion bead and occupied reorder beads on the same spatial edge.
The delete notch makes removal visible, but the prototype also exposes the unresolved conflict with cable dragging.

fr1.evidence: All mutations are one direct pointer gesture on the edge.

fr2.evidence: Dragging an occupied port bead is also the established cable-start gesture, so the prototype cannot predict intent without a modifier or mode.

fr3.evidence: Hollow and occupied points are legible once the Block is selected, though delete still needs a legend.

fr4.evidence: The control rail adds almost no occlusion and preserves the whole Block.

fr5.evidence: Small perimeter points and modifier deletion degrade at dense scales and on touch.

g1.evidence: FAIL: the occupied bead still carries both cable-start and reorder semantics; the prototype has not proven a non-ambiguous threshold.

g2.evidence: The trash notch can show the connected-cable count and one-step Undo.

g3.evidence: A stretched edge can render the same bead rail in Expanded view.

g4.evidence: Slot snapping reorders ids without recreating the port records.

variants.name: Port Tool
variants.thesis: Give port editing one explicit, persistent canvas mode: press P or choose Ports, then click gaps, drag rows, and delete without colliding with wiring.
variants.bestWhen: Several port edits happen in a burst and preserving predictable canvas gestures matters more than avoiding a mode.
variants.losesWhen: Most sessions make only one tiny edit and entering or exiting a dedicated tool feels like ceremony.

decisions.label: Primary object
decisions.value: Port editing is a first-class tldraw tool state, parallel to drawing or text tools.

decisions.label: Mode boundary
decisions.value: P or a labeled Ports pill enters; Escape or selecting another tool exits.

decisions.label: Within mode
decisions.value: Gap pluses, row grips, and trash are all explicit; cable creation is disabled until exit.

proof: The hero visibly changes the selected Block boundary when Port mode becomes active and exposes a dedicated edit rail.
Add, move, and delete map onto separate mode-owned controls while the cable tool remains outside the mode.

fr1.evidence: One mode entry amortizes across an arbitrary burst of single-action adds, moves, and deletes.

fr2.evidence: Port-list mutation is impossible outside the labeled tool and cable dragging is unavailable inside it.

fr3.evidence: The labeled Ports pill and mode outline are clear, though the P shortcut is learned rather than self-evident.

fr4.evidence: The Block and canvas remain visible; only a narrow rail and mode outline are added.

fr5.evidence: The tool can own large hit targets, keyboard traversal, pen behavior, and dense-list scrolling consistently.

g1.evidence: Port mode disables cable-start behavior; exiting restores the normal semantic terminal drag.

g2.evidence: Deleting a connected port opens an in-mode impact chip and commits through one Undo point.

g3.evidence: The same tool projects controls onto Port rows or Expanded edge positions.

g4.evidence: The tool dispatches moveBlockPort against durable ids and brackets each gesture as one history unit.

variants.name: Hold Lens
variants.thesis: Press-hold any port row to temporarily transform the Block into a large-target port-only lens; release to return to the sketch.
variants.bestWhen: A transient focus state should make dense ports easy to manipulate without leaving a lasting canvas mode.
variants.losesWhen: Hold duration is hard to discover or repeated edits outlast the comfortable pointer hold.

decisions.label: Primary object
decisions.value: The Block temporarily becomes a focused list while its title and footprint remain anchored.

decisions.label: Entry/exit
decisions.value: Hold crosses a visible dwell ring; pointer release or Escape restores the normal face.

decisions.label: Targets
decisions.value: Rows expand to large grips, labels, types, insertion boundaries, and delete buttons.

proof: The live hero swaps the body to a focused list without moving the Block or opening external chrome.
The lens exposes direct add/move/delete targets and then collapses back to the same face.

fr1.evidence: Actions are fast inside the lens, but entry must be repeated if the hold is released between edits.

fr2.evidence: A dwell ring and transformed face establish intent, though hold timing remains a threshold interaction.

fr3.evidence: The row reacts once held, but a new user may not know that a hold exists.

fr4.evidence: The lens occupies only the Block's own footprint and intentionally hides irrelevant internals during editing.

fr5.evidence: Large targets help touch and density, while keyboard users need an explicit command to lock the transient lens.

g1.evidence: The dwell completes on the row label/gutter, never the cable dot, and the transformed lens suspends wiring.

g2.evidence: The lens has an explicit trash cell with cable impact and one-step Undo.

g3.evidence: Expanded view can transform only its boundary layer while fading interior content.

g4.evidence: List operations keep ids and the hold lifecycle brackets each commit cleanly.

variants.name: Row Commands
variants.thesis: Keep the canvas visually unchanged and put the complete add-above/below, move, duplicate, and delete vocabulary in the port context menu.
variants.bestWhen: A reliable accessible command path matters more than peak repeated-edit speed or persistent visual affordances.
variants.losesWhen: Many ports are being rearranged and reopening a menu per action becomes tedious.

decisions.label: Primary object
decisions.value: Each port is a command target; the menu is the canonical invocation surface.

decisions.label: Ordering
decisions.value: Move up/down commands avoid drag precision and gain keyboard shortcuts.

decisions.label: Delete
decisions.value: The menu can state the exact cable impact before the destructive item is chosen.

proof: The hero opens a row-anchored command menu beside out_1 and drives add, move, and delete states from real menu items.
No controls occupy the Block until the row command is invoked.

fr1.evidence: Every operation exists, but repeated changes reopen and traverse the menu.

fr2.evidence: Commands are explicit, target-bound, and separate from cable or selection gestures.

fr3.evidence: Right-click is familiar, but the operation set remains invisible until invoked.

fr4.evidence: The normal canvas has zero added chrome; the temporary menu is row-anchored.

fr5.evidence: Keyboard shortcuts and menu targets scale well, though touch needs a long-press or visible overflow trigger.

g1.evidence: The context trigger is a secondary click or overflow button; direct port drag always starts a cable.

g2.evidence: The delete item can read ‘Delete port and 1 cable’ and map to one undoable command.

g3.evidence: Commands operate on a selected semantic port independent of its rendered y position.

g4.evidence: All entries call the existing id-based command layer with explicit history labels.

variants.name: Port Sheet
variants.thesis: Open a compact spreadsheet-like editor anchored over the Block, with large rows, drag grips, types, and add/delete controls in one stable surface.
variants.bestWhen: The list is dense or typed, several properties must be edited together, and one local overlay is acceptable.
variants.losesWhen: Preserving a completely unobscured view of the Block and nearby cables is more important than list control.

decisions.label: Primary object
decisions.value: A compact two-kind table treats Inputs and Outputs as editable records.

decisions.label: Surface
decisions.value: The footer's Ports button opens an anchored sheet rather than the distant inspector.

decisions.label: Scale
decisions.value: The sheet can scroll, expose types/defaults, and support keyboard row navigation.

proof: The hero opens a real anchored sheet inside the canvas and keeps the decode title visibly behind it.
Add, move, and delete all remain available without reopening the surface.

fr1.evidence: One sheet opening amortizes across rapid row operations, though it adds an entry click.

fr2.evidence: Every mutation has a labeled table control and the canvas cable gesture is untouched.

fr3.evidence: The labeled Ports footer and conventional table controls expose the full interaction.

fr4.evidence: The sheet is local but covers most of the Block body and some nearby canvas.

fr5.evidence: Large scrollable rows, keyboard focus, and type fields are the most robust dense-list surface.

g1.evidence: All sheet interactions occur off the port terminal, leaving direct cable drag unchanged.

g2.evidence: The trash cell can disclose connection impact and retain an Undo action in the sheet footer.

g3.evidence: The sheet edits semantic records and therefore behaves identically for Port and Expanded rendering.

g4.evidence: Rows bind to stable ids, and each manipulation is one named command/history unit.

variants.name: Keyboard List
variants.thesis: Let the Block's port region enter a text-like list editor: Enter adds, Alt+Arrow reorders, and Backspace deletes the focused port.
variants.bestWhen: Expert keyboard throughput, port naming, and accessible deterministic focus matter more than first-use pointer discoverability.
variants.losesWhen: The user expects purely spatial manipulation or rarely uses shortcuts.

decisions.label: Primary object
decisions.value: Ports are editable lines with a caret, selection, and familiar text-list commands.

decisions.label: Entry
decisions.value: Double-click a label or press Enter on a selected port; Escape returns to canvas selection.

decisions.label: Mutation
decisions.value: Enter, Alt+Arrow, and Backspace map to add, move, and delete while inline naming remains available.

proof: The hero swaps the body into a compact line editor and exposes active focus plus actual shortcut controls.
The same ordered list state drives the add, move, and delete examples.

fr1.evidence: After entry, an expert can add/name/reorder/delete without leaving the keyboard.

fr2.evidence: A focused editor state owns keyboard mutation while pointer terminal dragging remains unchanged.

fr3.evidence: The entry and shortcut vocabulary are poorly discoverable without a hint or command menu.

fr4.evidence: The editor replaces only the Block body and preserves its title, footprint, and canvas context.

fr5.evidence: Deterministic focus, large line rows, screen-reader labels, and no pointer precision make this exceptionally robust.

g1.evidence: The editor begins only from label focus/Enter; pointer dragging the terminal remains a cable action.

g2.evidence: Backspace on a connected row opens an inline impact confirmation and one Undo unit.

g3.evidence: Both visual views project the same ordered list into this editor state.

g4.evidence: Caret rows are keyed by id and Alt+Arrow mutates order without recreation.

variants.name: Port Halo
variants.thesis: Select one port, then expose a tiny adjacent halo with add-above/below, move, and delete actions bound to that exact target.
variants.bestWhen: Single precise edits dominate and the UI should explicitly show which port each action will affect.
variants.losesWhen: Many ports must be reordered because each operation begins with a new target selection.

decisions.label: Primary object
decisions.value: One selected port owns a small contextual action cluster.

decisions.label: Target clarity
decisions.value: The selected row highlights before any add, move, or delete command is offered.

decisions.label: Dismissal
decisions.value: Clicking canvas, Escape, or starting a cable hides the halo immediately.

proof: The hero highlights out_1 and opens a compact vertical halo physically adjacent to that port.
Each button drives the shared add/move/delete list states and keeps the target visible.

fr1.evidence: Single edits are fast, but repeated work incurs select-then-command cycles.

fr2.evidence: The explicit selection state and separate halo buttons make target and verb unambiguous.

fr3.evidence: Selecting a port reveals labeled-symbol controls exactly where the user is looking.

fr4.evidence: The halo stays beside the Block but temporarily occupies a narrow canvas gutter.

fr5.evidence: Large halo buttons and keyboard roving focus work well, though dense edges can make initial port selection difficult.

g1.evidence: Starting a cable dismisses the halo; halo actions live outside the terminal dot.

g2.evidence: The selected target lets delete show an exact impact count and one-step Undo.

g3.evidence: The halo anchors to whichever semantic port position the current view projects.

g4.evidence: Commands address the selected stable id and bracket history per action.

variants.name: Typed Tokens
variants.thesis: Open a tiny palette of typed port tokens and drag one onto a highlighted Block edge; rearrange tokens spatially and drop them into Trash.
variants.bestWhen: Choosing a port type while adding is common and direct spatial placement is more valuable than compact menus.
variants.losesWhen: Pointer travel, touch precision, or many reorder operations make drag-and-drop tiring.

decisions.label: Primary object
decisions.value: A port is a typed token inserted onto a spatial drop edge.

decisions.label: Creation
decisions.value: Drag Input, Image, or Text from a local palette to the exact side and slot.

decisions.label: Move/delete
decisions.value: Drag a row to another slot or into a visible Trash token while edit state is active.

proof: The hero opens a typed palette and exposes a dashed insertion edge directly on the Block.
The shared states demonstrate a typed in_2 addition, spatial reorder, and explicit Trash drop.

fr1.evidence: Typed add combines creation and type choice, but drag travel slows repeated reorder and delete.

fr2.evidence: The palette/drop-edge state establishes intent, though dragging existing ports still needs an edit-state rule.

fr3.evidence: The palette labels types and the dashed edge advertises a drop target, but its launcher must first be found.

fr4.evidence: The palette stays local and the Block remains visible, with modest gutter occlusion.

fr5.evidence: Spatial drag is clear at moderate density but needs command fallbacks for keyboard, touch, and long Expanded edges.

g1.evidence: The highlighted drop edge appears only after opening the palette; ordinary terminal drag outside that state remains wiring.

g2.evidence: Trash is a labeled drop target with cable impact and a one-step Undo toast.

g3.evidence: Tokens target semantic side/order and can drop onto compact or stretched edge projections.

g4.evidence: Drops resolve to id-based create/move/remove commands with one history boundary.

variants.name: Footer Strip
variants.thesis: Put a quiet but permanent +Input, +Output, Reorder, and Delete strip in the Block footer so the core operations are always one click away.
variants.bestWhen: The fastest learnable default matters and a small amount of persistent Block chrome is acceptable.
variants.losesWhen: Hundreds of Blocks make the repeated footer controls visually noisy or the footer width becomes constrained.

decisions.label: Primary object
decisions.value: The existing Block footer becomes the stable command home for port-list edits.

decisions.label: Creation
decisions.value: Separate +Input and +Output buttons remove side/type ambiguity.

decisions.label: Ordering/delete
decisions.value: Reorder enters an obvious numbered state; Delete applies to the selected port and is disabled without one.

proof: The live hero uses the Block's already-existing 46px footer and adds no popover or external surface.
All three operations are visible in the starting state and drive the same port-list mutations.

fr1.evidence: Add is always one click and reorder/delete are shallow, though target selection adds a step.

fr2.evidence: Labeled footer buttons are separate from every port, selection, text, and cable gesture.

fr3.evidence: The complete operation vocabulary is visible without hover, hold, shortcut, or secondary click.

fr4.evidence: The strip stays inside an existing footer but adds persistent visual weight to every editable Block.

fr5.evidence: Large labeled buttons and keyboard focus are robust, while narrow Blocks need overflow or responsive compaction.

g1.evidence: All mutations start in the footer, so terminal dragging is exclusively cable creation.

g2.evidence: Delete activates only after a port selection and can state the affected cable count before one-step commit.

g3.evidence: The footer persists in both Port and Expanded views and targets semantic records.

g4.evidence: Commands call stable-id mutations and one named history step each.

story.title: Keep every port command one click away

steps.label: See all commands
steps.caption: The existing footer permanently exposes the complete edit vocabulary.

steps.label: Add an Input
steps.caption: A labeled one-click command inserts in_2 with no menu or gesture discovery.

steps.label: Enter reorder
steps.caption: The footer's reorder command makes the temporary ordering state explicit.

steps.label: Delete selected
steps.caption: Trash is available only after a port target is selected and remains undoable.

media.label: Persistent command home
media.caption: The strip trades a small permanent footprint for immediate first-use comprehension and predictable keyboard access.
